notes.meaning: Ahab had seventy male descendants living in the royal city of Samaria. Before marching there, Jehu sent letters to the city officials, elders, and the guardians caring for the young princes. He wanted to test where their loyalties lay before taking his next step.

Jehu challenged the leaders to pick the best royal son, crown him king, and fight to defend Ahab's dynasty. He pointed out that they had horses, chariots, weapons, and a fortified city to defend themselves. He spoke with sharp irony to dare them to resist, forcing them to show if they had any courage to oppose him.

The leaders of Samaria were overcome with terror when they read the letter. They reasoned that if two kings, Joram and Ahaziah, could not stand against Jehu, they had no chance of surviving a battle with him. Their fear was purely practical, thinking only of their own safety rather than turning to God.

The palace manager, the city governor, the elders, and the princes' guardians quickly surrendered to Jehu. They promised to be his servants, refuse to crown any king, and obey whatever he ordered. Out of self-preservation, the very men charged with protecting Ahab's heirs abandoned them completely.

Jehu sent back a second letter demanding absolute proof of their allegiance. He ordered them to cut off the heads of Ahab's seventy descendants and bring them to him at Jezreel by the next day. By forcing these officials to carry out the executions, Jehu bound them directly to his rebellion.

When the leaders received the order, they murdered all seventy of the king's sons and grandsons under their care. They packed the severed heads into baskets and delivered them to Jehu at Jezreel. These leaders proved that people who do not fear God will readily betray those entrusted to their care.

When the messenger reported that the heads had arrived, Jehu directed that they be piled into two heaps at the city gate until morning. The city gate was the public center of community life and judgment. Leaving the heaps there served as a grim warning to everyone that resisting Jehu was hopeless.

The next morning, Jehu stood before the crowd and told the people they were innocent of treason. He admitted that he had conspired against and killed King Joram, but asked who had killed all these princes. By asking this, he publicly exposed the Samarian leaders' guilt and defended his own uprising.

Jehu declared that every single word the Lord had spoken against Ahab's house would come to pass. God was fulfilling the exact judgment He had announced earlier through the prophet Elijah. Jehu reminded the people that behind all the human violence, God's righteous word was being carried out.

Jehu wiped out everyone connected to Ahab who remained in Jezreel. This targeted purge included Ahab's prominent officials, close friends, and the priests who supported his idolatry. He left no survivors of that wicked royal household in the city.
Jehu left Jezreel and journeyed toward Samaria to finish his mission. Along the road, he stopped at Beth-eked of the Shepherds, a place where local shepherds gathered to tie up and shear their sheep.

Jehu met forty-two relatives of King Ahaziah of Judah, who were traveling to visit their royal family, unaware of the rebellion. Because they were related to Ahab through marriage and allied with his family, Jehu captured them alive and had them killed at the pit. God's judgment reached even those from Judah who had joined themselves to Ahab's wickedness.

differ.view: Some view Jehu as exceeding God's commission here, slaughtering Ahaziah's relatives out of personal ambition rather than divine command.

notes.meaning: Jehu met Jehonadab son of Rechab, a respected man known for strict devotion and simple living. After confirming they shared the same commitment against Ahab's dynasty, Jehu took his hand and invited him into his chariot to see his zeal for the Lord. Riding with such a holy man helped Jehu win public support, though Jehu also displayed an urge to show off his own deeds.

Upon reaching Samaria, Jehu slaughtered every remaining person belonging to Ahab's family. He did not stop until the entire dynasty in the capital was wiped out. This completely fulfilled the judgment that the Lord had spoken to Elijah years before.

Jehu assembled the people and announced that while Ahab had served the false god Baal a little, he would serve him greatly. This bold statement was completely untrue and designed to trap Baal's followers. He feigned devotion so the idolaters would drop their guard and assemble together.

Jehu commanded every prophet, priest, and worshipper of Baal to attend a massive sacrifice, warning that anyone absent would be put to death. The death penalty ensured that nobody would dare stay away. The text clearly states that Jehu acted with cunning deceit to bring about their destruction.

Jehu ordered a solemn religious assembly in honor of Baal, and his officials proclaimed it throughout the realm. A solemn assembly was a sacred gathering where ordinary work was set aside. This formal announcement convinced the worshippers of Baal that a genuine national revival of their cult was underway.

Word spread across the entire land of Israel, and every single worshipper of Baal came to Samaria. They packed into the temple of Baal until the building was filled from one end to the other, like a jar filled to the brim. The false worshippers felt secure and delighted, unaware that their gathering was a trap.

Jehu instructed the keeper of the temple wardrobe to bring out sacred vestments for all the worshippers. Special robes were customary for serving Baal, and having everyone wear them added to the ceremony. It also marked out every follower of Baal clearly, making it impossible for anyone to hide in the crowd.

Jehu entered the temple with Jehonadab and told the crowd to make sure no worshipper of the Lord was among them. The crowd thought this was done out of reverence to keep their temple unpolluted by outsiders. In truth, Jehu wanted to protect innocent worshippers of the Lord from being killed along with the idolaters.

As the priests began offering the sacrifices, Jehu stationed eighty trusted guards outside with orders that anyone who let a worshipper escape would pay with his own life. As soon as the offering ended, the guards charged in, slaughtered everyone with the sword, threw out the bodies, and pushed into the inner shrine. God's law demanded death for idolatry, and Jehu executed the penalty completely.

The soldiers dragged out the sacred wooden pillars from the temple and burned them in the fire. Then they smashed the main stone pillar of Baal, demolished the temple building, and turned the site into a public latrine. Turning the sacred ground into an open sewer brought total, lasting dishonor to the idol's memory.

Through these drastic measures, Jehu completely wiped out the worship of Baal from the northern kingdom. No other king in northern Israel took such aggressive action against that foreign cult. It was a remarkable outward purge of a terrible spiritual poison.

Even after destroying Baal, Jehu refused to abandon the royal golden-calf shrines set up at Bethel and Dan by Jeroboam. Jeroboam had introduced these calves as a state religion to keep Israelites from traveling south to Jerusalem to worship. Jehu preserved this convenient political worship, proving that his religious reforms were driven partly by personal politics rather than pure devotion to God.

The Lord spoke to Jehu and commended him for carrying out His judgment against the wicked family of Ahab. Because he executed this assignment, God promised that four generations of his descendants would sit upon Israel's throne. God fairly rewarded Jehu's public service, giving his family the longest-lasting dynasty in the northern kingdom.

Despite his early zeal, Jehu did not take care to obey the law of the Lord with all his heart. He clung to the golden calves of Jeroboam and never truly sought God's will. A person can perform great external tasks for God and still lack a genuine, undivided heart for Him.

Because Israel continued in unfaithfulness, the Lord began to shrink their national territory. King Hazael of Syria attacked their borders and conquered all the Israelite land east of the Jordan River. This included the entire territories of Gad, Reuben, and eastern Manasseh, fulfilling earlier prophetic warnings of Syrian oppression.

The rest of Jehu's deeds, his military power, and his achievements were preserved in the royal records of Israel's kings. Jehu died after reigning twenty-eight years in Samaria, was buried with his ancestors, and his son Jehoahaz succeeded him. Though his reign was long and began with dramatic victories, it ended with a nation diminished and spiritually compromised.
